title: Θέτιδος λιταὶ καὶ ἀσπίς
titleEn: The Plea and the Shield — Iliad 18.410–508
about: Hephaestus rises limping from his anvil, puts away his tools, washes, dresses, and comes out leaning on golden handmaids that think, speak and work like living girls. He greets Thetis and offers to do whatever she asks. Weeping, she tells her sorrows: Zeus married her against her will to a mortal, Peleus, now worn out with age; her son, the best of the heroes, is short-lived and grieving; his prize was taken from him, he refused the elders’ gifts, and Patroclus, sent out in his armour, has been killed by Apollo and his armour lost. She begs new armour for Achilles. Hephaestus promises it at once, sets his twenty bellows to work, and begins the shield: on it earth, sky and sea, the sun, the moon and the stars, and two cities of men. In the first a wedding procession goes through the streets, and in the place of assembly two men dispute the price of a man’s death before the elders.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ ἀπ’ ἀκμοθέτοιο πέλωρ αἴητον ἀνέστη
χωλεύων·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and from the anvil-block the monster, huge, rose up,
limping;
sentences.i: So he said, and the huge monster rose up from the anvil-block, limping;
sentences.n: ἦ, καί is the speech-closing ‘He spoke, and’: ἦ is an old past of ἠμί ‘say’. ἀκμόθετον is the block on which the anvil (ἄκμων) is set, from τίθημι ‘set’, and ἀπ’ ἀκμοθέτοιο has the epic genitive -οιο. πέλωρ ‘monster’ is said of the god himself, a being of portentous size. The meaning of αἴητον is not known: the ancient explanation is ‘huge’, which the English follows, and ‘panting’ (from ἄημι ‘blow’) has also been guessed. χωλεύων ‘limping’ is the participle of χωλεύω; Hephaestus is lame (χωλός, 397).

sentences.t: ὑπὸ δὲ κνῆμαι ῥώοντο ἀραιαί.
sentences.l: and beneath him his shins moved nimbly, slender ones.
sentences.i: and beneath him his slender shins moved nimbly.
sentences.n: ὑπό is an adverb, ‘beneath (him)’. ῥώοντο is the imperfect of ῥώομαι ‘move quickly, nimbly’, and κνῆμαι are the shins, the lower legs. ἀραιαί ‘slender, thin’ stands at the end of the sentence: the legs are thin but quick, under a heavy upper body (415).

sentences.t:
φύσας μέν ῥ’ ἀπάνευθε τίθει πυρός, ὅπλά τε πάντα
λάρνακ’ ἐς ἀργυρέην συλλέξατο, τοῖς ἐπονεῖτο·
sentences.l:
The bellows he set away from the fire, and all the gear
into a silver chest he gathered, with which he toiled;
sentences.i: He set the bellows away from the fire, and gathered all the gear he toiled with into a silver chest;
sentences.n: This is what he said he would do at 409. τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι ‘set’, with ἀπάνευθε … πυρός ‘away from the fire’. ὅπλα is the smith’s ‘gear’, and συλλέξατο an unaugmented aorist middle of συλλέγω ‘gather together’. λάρνακ’ is λάρνακα, ‘chest, box’. τοῖς ἐπονεῖτο is ‘with which he toiled’: τοῖς is a relative here, a dative of means, and πονέομαι is ‘toil’.

sentences.t:
σπόγγῳ δ’ ἀμφὶ πρόσωπα καὶ ἄμφω χεῖρ’ ἀπομόργνυ
αὐχένα τε στιβαρὸν καὶ στήθεα λαχνήεντα,
δῦ δὲ χιτῶν’, ἕλε δὲ σκῆπτρον παχύ, βῆ δὲ θύραζε
χωλεύων·
sentences.l:
And with a sponge about his face and both his hands he wiped,
and his neck, stout, and his chest, hairy,
and he put on a tunic, and took a sceptre, thick, and went outside
limping;
sentences.i: With a sponge he wiped his face and both his hands, his stout neck and his hairy chest, and he put on a tunic, took a thick sceptre, and went outside, limping;
sentences.n: ἀπομόργνυ is the imperfect of ἀπομόργνυμι ‘wipe off’, and its objects run on into the next line: πρόσωπα ‘face’ (plural in Homer), χεῖρ’ (the dual χεῖρε, ‘both hands’, with ἄμφω), αὐχένα ‘neck’, στήθεα ‘chest’. στιβαρόν ‘stout’ and λαχνήεντα ‘hairy’ describe the smith’s body. Three short clauses follow with δέ: δῦ (unaugmented aorist of δύω) ‘put on’, ἕλε ‘took’, βῆ ‘went’. θύραζε is ‘to the door, outside’. χωλεύων ‘limping’ ends the sentence as it ended the first one (411).

sentences.t:
ὑπὸ δ’ ἀμφίπολοι ῥώοντο ἄνακτι
χρύσειαι ζωῇσι νεήνισιν εἰοικυῖαι.
sentences.l:
and beneath, handmaids moved nimbly for their lord,
golden ones, like living young women.
sentences.i: and handmaids moved nimbly beneath their lord to support him, made of gold, like living young women.
sentences.n: ὑπό is again ‘beneath’, and ῥώοντο is the same verb as in 411: as his legs moved nimbly under him, so do the handmaids, holding him up. ἄνακτι is the dative of ἄναξ ‘lord’, ‘for their lord’. χρύσειαι ‘golden’ is the surprise: they are made, not born. ζωῇσι νεήνισιν is ‘living young women’, with ζωός ‘alive’ in the epic dative plural -ῃσι; εἰοικυῖαι is the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, with the dative.

sentences.t:
τῇς ἐν μὲν νόος ἐστὶ μετὰ φρεσίν, ἐν δὲ καὶ αὐδὴ
καὶ σθένος, ἀθανάτων δὲ θεῶν ἄπο ἔργα ἴσασιν.
sentences.l:
In them there is a mind within their wits, and in them also voice
and strength, and from the immortal gods they know works.
sentences.i: There is a mind in their wits, and they have voice and strength, and from the immortal gods they know the works of skill.
sentences.n: τῇς is an epic dative plural (= ταῖς), ‘in them’, picked up by ἐν μέν … ἐν δέ, where ἐν is an adverb, ‘within’. νόος is ‘mind’ and φρένες ‘wits’. αὐδή is ‘voice, speech’, and σθένος ‘strength’. θεῶν ἄπο, with the accent thrown back on the preposition placed after its noun, is ‘from the gods’: their skill was taught them by the gods. ἴσασιν is the third plural of οἶδα ‘know’. ἔργα is ‘works’, here skilled work.

sentences.t: αἳ μὲν ὕπαιθα ἄνακτος ἐποίπνυον·
sentences.l: They were bustling beneath their lord;
sentences.i: They bustled about at their lord’s side, holding him up;
sentences.n: αἳ μέν is ‘they’, the handmaids, answered by αὐτὰρ ὅ ‘but he’. ὕπαιθα is ‘beneath’ or ‘at the side of’, with the genitive ἄνακτος; the picture is of the girls supporting him as he walks. ἐποίπνυον is the imperfect of ποιπνύω ‘bustle, be busy’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ ἔρρων
πλησίον, ἔνθα Θέτις περ, ἐπὶ θρόνου ἷζε φαεινοῦ,
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρὶ ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l:
but he, going painfully
near, where Thetis was, upon a shining chair sat,
and he clasped her by the hand, and spoke a word, and called her by name:
sentences.i: but he made his painful way close to where Thetis was, and sat down on a shining chair, and took her hand, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: ἔρρων is the participle of ἔρρω, a verb of going with difficulty or ill fortune; of the lame god it is ‘going painfully’. πλησίον ‘near’ goes with ἔνθα Θέτις περ ‘(to) where Thetis was’, and περ simply stresses the place. ἷζε is the imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit’, with ἐπὶ θρόνου … φαεινοῦ ‘on a shining chair’, the adjective held to the end of the line. The last line is the formula for taking someone by the hand to speak, with ἔν … φῦ (from ἐμφύω ‘cling to’) and ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε each split by tmesis; it takes the English it has elsewhere, with ‘her’ for ‘him’.

sentences.t:
τίπτε Θέτι τανύπεπλε ἱκάνεις ἡμέτερον δῶ
αἰδοίη τε φίλη τε; πάρος γε μὲν οὔ τι θαμίζεις.
sentences.l:
“Why, long-robed Thetis, have you come to our house,
revered and dear? Before, at least, you do not at all come often.
sentences.i: “Why have you come to our house, long-robed Thetis, revered and dear? Before now, at least, you have not been a frequent visitor.
sentences.n: Hephaestus greets Thetis with the very words his wife Charis used at 385–386, and the English is the same. Θέτι τανύπεπλε is vocative, ‘long-robed Thetis’. τίπτε is ‘why, pray’. ἱκάνεις has the force of a perfect, ‘have come’, and δῶ is short for δῶμα ‘house’. αἰδοίη τε φίλη τε ‘revered and dear’ agree with Θέτι. θαμίζεις ‘you come often’ has the negative οὔ τι ‘not at all’.

sentences.t: αὔδα ὅ τι φρονέεις·
sentences.l: Speak what you have in mind;
sentences.i: Speak what you have in mind;
sentences.n: αὔδα is the present imperative of αὐδάω ‘speak, say’, and ὅ τι φρονέεις ‘what you have in mind’ uses the uncontracted φρονέεις (= φρονεῖς). Aphrodite says the same words to Hera at 14.195, and they keep the English they have there; the half-line also stands alone in the Odyssey (5.89, Calypso to Hermes), where it is rendered ‘Say what you have in mind’.

sentences.t:
τελέσαι δέ με θυμὸς ἄνωγεν,
εἰ δύναμαι τελέσαι γε καὶ εἰ τετελεσμένον ἐστίν.
sentences.l:
and to accomplish it my heart bids me,
if I am able to accomplish it, and if it is a thing accomplishable.”
sentences.i: and my heart urges me to do it, if I can, and if it is a thing that is meant to be done.”
sentences.n: These are the words with which Aphrodite answered Hera at 14.195–196, and they keep the English they have there. ἄνωγεν is a perfect with present sense, ‘bids’. τετελεσμένον, the perfect passive participle of τελέω, is here ‘able to be accomplished’. γε after τελέσαι stresses the condition: ‘if I can do it at all’. Hephaestus’ short speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Θέτις κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα·
sentences.l: Him then answered Thetis, down a tear shedding:
sentences.i: Then Thetis answered him, shedding tears:
sentences.n: The reply formula for Thetis, with κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα ‘shedding a tear’, κατά standing apart from its verb (tmesis). τόν is ‘him’, the article used as a pronoun. ἠμείβετ’ is ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, elided.

sentences.l:
“Hephaestus, is there then indeed any, of all the goddesses who are on Olympus,
who so many in her own wits has endured, grievous sorrows,
as the pains that to me beyond all the son of Cronus, Zeus, has given?
sentences.i: “Hephaestus, is there any goddess, of all who are on Olympus, who has endured in her mind so many grievous sorrows as the pains that Zeus, the son of Cronus, has given me beyond them all?
sentences.n: Thetis opens with a question that expects the answer ‘no’. ἦ ἄρα δή is ‘is it then really so that…?’, and τις ‘any (goddess)’ is defined by ὅσαι θεαί … ‘of all the goddesses who…’. τοσσάδ’ (= τοσάδε) ‘so many’ is answered by ὅσσ’ ‘as many as’. ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ᾗσιν is ‘in her own wits’, with the possessive ὅς in the epic dative plural. ἀνέσχετο is the aorist of ἀνέχομαι ‘hold up under, endure’. ἐκ πασέων is ‘out of all (the goddesses)’, ‘beyond all’, with the epic genitive plural -έων.

sentences.t:
ἐκ μέν μ’ ἀλλάων ἁλιάων ἀνδρὶ δάμασσεν
Αἰακίδῃ Πηλῆϊ, καὶ ἔτλην ἀνέρος εὐνὴν
πολλὰ μάλ’ οὐκ ἐθέλουσα.
sentences.l:
Out of the other women of the sea, me he subdued to a man,
to the descendant of Aeacus, Peleus, and I endured a man’s bed,
very much unwilling.
sentences.i: Out of all the other women of the sea he subdued me to a man, to Peleus, descendant of Aeacus, and I endured a man’s bed, much against my will.
sentences.n: The subject is still Zeus. ἐκ … ἀλλάων ἁλιάων is ‘out of the other women of the sea’, the Nereids, Thetis’ sisters; ἀλλάων and ἁλιάων are epic genitive plurals in -άων (= -ῶν). δάμασσεν, aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, is used of a goddess given to a husband, as of a horse broken to the yoke. Αἰακίδης ‘descendant of Aeacus’ is the house rendering; Peleus is Aeacus’ son. ἔτλην is the aorist of τλάω ‘endure’, and ἀνέρος (= ἀνδρός) εὐνήν is ‘a man’s bed’, a mortal’s. πολλὰ μάλ’ is an adverb, ‘very much’, with οὐκ ἐθέλουσα ‘unwilling’.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν δὴ γήραϊ λυγρῷ
κεῖται ἐνὶ μεγάροις ἀρημένος, ἄλλα δέ μοι νῦν·
sentences.l:
He indeed, by grievous old age
lies in the halls worn down, and now other things are mine;
sentences.i: He lies in his halls, worn out by grievous old age, and now I have other sorrows:
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν δή is ‘he’, Peleus, with the article as a pronoun. γήραϊ λυγρῷ ‘by grievous old age’ is a dative of cause, and γήραϊ is the epic dative of γῆρας. ἀρημένος is an old participle of uncertain derivation, rendered ‘worn down’ as in the Odyssey. ἄλλα δέ μοι νῦν leaves out a verb: ‘and now there are other (sorrows) for me’, set out in the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
υἱὸν ἐπεί μοι δῶκε γενέσθαί τε τραφέμεν τε
ἔξοχον ἡρώων·
sentences.l:
since he gave me a son to be born and to be reared,
standing out above the heroes;
sentences.i: since he granted me a son, born and reared to stand out above the heroes;
sentences.n: υἱὸν ἐπεί is ἐπεὶ υἱόν with the object placed first. δῶκε, unaugmented, still has Zeus as its subject, and the infinitives γενέσθαι ‘to be born’ and τραφέμεν ‘to be reared’ (an epic infinitive in -έμεν, from τρέφω) say what he granted. ἔξοχον ἡρώων ‘standing out above the heroes’ is the phrase Thetis used at 56, with the genitive of comparison.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἀνέδραμεν ἔρνεϊ ἶσος·
sentences.l: and he ran up equal to a sapling;
sentences.i: and he sprang up like a young sapling;
sentences.n: The half-line is the one at 56, and it keeps its English. ἀνέδραμεν, aorist of ἀνατρέχω ‘run up’, is said of quick growth, and ἔρνεϊ ἶσος ‘equal to a sapling’ has the dative after ἶσος.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ θρέψασα φυτὸν ὣς γουνῷ ἀλωῆς
νηυσὶν ἐπιπροέηκα κορωνίσιν Ἴλιον εἴσω
Τρωσὶ μαχησόμενον·
sentences.i: I reared him like a plant on the rich ground of an orchard, and sent him forth in the curved ships to Ilium to fight the Trojans;
sentences.n: Lines 438–443 repeat Thetis’ words to her sisters at 57–62, and keep their English. θρέψασα is the aorist participle of τρέφω ‘rear’, and φυτὸν ὥς ‘like a plant’ has ὡς after its noun. γουνῷ ἀλωῆς is ‘on the rich ground of an orchard’; the sense of γουνός is not certain. ἐπιπροέηκα is the aorist of ἐπιπροΐημι ‘send forth’, and μαχησόμενον a future participle of purpose.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὐχ ὑποδέξομαι αὖτις
οἴκαδε νοστήσαντα δόμον Πηλήϊον εἴσω.
sentences.l:
but him I shall not receive again
returned home into the house of Peleus.
sentences.i: but I shall not receive him back again, returned home into the house of Peleus.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ answers τὸν μέν: ‘but him’. ὑποδέξομαι is future, ‘I shall receive’. νοστήσαντα is the aorist participle of νοστέω ‘come home’, and δόμον Πηλήϊον εἴσω is ‘into the house of Peleus’, with the adjective Πηλήϊος for the genitive.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα δέ μοι ζώει καὶ ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο
ἄχνυται, οὐδέ τί οἱ δύναμαι χραισμῆσαι ἰοῦσα.
sentences.l:
But while he lives for me and sees the light of the sun,
he is grieved, and I cannot at all help him by going.
sentences.i: But while he lives and sees the light of the sun, he is grieved, and I cannot help him at all by going to him.
sentences.n: ὄφρα is ‘so long as’, and μοι ‘for me’ is a dative of interest. ζώει is epic for ζῇ ‘lives’, and ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο ‘sees the light of the sun’ is to be alive. ἄχνυται is ‘is grieved’. χραισμῆσαι ‘to help’ takes the dative οἱ ‘him’, and ἰοῦσα, a participle of εἶμι, is ‘by going’.

sentences.t:
κούρην ἣν ἄρα οἱ γέρας ἔξελον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
τὴν ἂψ ἐκ χειρῶν ἕλετο κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων.
sentences.l:
The girl whom as a prize to him the sons of the Achaeans picked out,
her back from his hands took lord Agamemnon.
sentences.i: The girl whom the sons of the Achaeans picked out as his prize of honour, her lord Agamemnon took back out of his hands.
sentences.n: The two lines are Achilles’ own words at 16.56 and 16.58, with οἱ ‘for him’ in place of μοι ‘for me’; the English is the same, made third person. The girl is Briseis, not named. κούρην ἣν ‘the girl whom’ is picked up by τήν ‘her’ in the next line. ἔξελον is the aorist of ἐξαιρέω ‘pick out’, with γέρας ‘prize’ as predicate. κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘lord Agamemnon’.

sentences.t: ἤτοι ὃ τῆς ἀχέων φρένας ἔφθιεν·
sentences.l: He indeed, grieving for her, was wasting away in his wits;
sentences.i: Grieving for her, he was wasting away in his mind;
sentences.n: ἤτοι is ‘indeed’, printed as one word. ὅ is ‘he’, Achilles. τῆς ἀχέων is ‘grieving for her’, with the genitive of cause; ἀχέων is the participle of ἀχέω ‘grieve’. ἔφθιεν is the imperfect of φθίω ‘waste away’, and φρένας ‘in his wits’ is an accusative of respect; ἔφθιεν can also be taken as transitive, ‘was wasting his heart’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὺς
Τρῶες ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσιν ἐείλεον, οὐδὲ θύραζε
εἴων ἐξιέναι·
sentences.i: but the Trojans were penning the Achaeans in at the sterns of their ships, and would not let them go outside;
sentences.n: ἐείλεον is the imperfect of εἰλέω ‘hem in, pen in’. ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσιν is ‘at the sterns’, the ships drawn up on the beach with their sterns toward the land. εἴων is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘let, allow’, with οὐδέ ‘and not’, and ἐξιέναι ‘to go out’ is the infinitive of ἔξειμι. θύραζε ‘outside’ is the word used of Hephaestus going out at 416.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ λίσσοντο γέροντες
Ἀργείων, καὶ πολλὰ περικλυτὰ δῶρ’ ὀνόμαζον.
sentences.l:
and him the elders begged,
of the Argives, and many very famous gifts they named.
sentences.i: and the elders of the Argives begged him, and named many very famous gifts.
sentences.n: Thetis is telling the embassy of Book 9 in a line and a half. λίσσοντο is unaugmented (= ἐλίσσοντο) ‘begged’, with τόν ‘him’ as object. γέροντες Ἀργείων is ‘the elders of the Argives’. περικλυτὰ δῶρ’ ὀνόμαζον, ‘named very famous gifts’, recalls the words with which Agamemnon introduced his list at 9.121, περικλυτὰ δῶρ’ ὀνομήνω; ὀνομάζω is ‘name, list’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὐτὸς μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἠναίνετο λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι,
αὐτὰρ ὃ Πάτροκλον περὶ μὲν τὰ ἃ τεύχεα ἕσσε,
πέμπε δέ μιν πόλεμον δέ, πολὺν δ’ ἅμα λαὸν ὄπασσε.
sentences.l:
Then he himself rejected warding off the ruin,
but he clothed Patroclus about in his own armour,
and sent him to the war, and gave many people to go with him.
sentences.i: Then, though he himself rejected their plea to ward off ruin, he clothed Patroclus in his own armour and sent him into the war, and gave him many troops to go with him.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς μέν ‘he himself’ is set against αὐτὰρ ὅ … ‘but he (sent another)’. ἠναίνετο is the imperfect of ἀναίνομαι ‘reject’, and λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι is ‘to ward off ruin’. περὶ … ἕσσε is tmesis of περιέννυμι ‘clothe about’, with two accusatives, the man and the armour; τὰ ἅ is ‘his own’, the possessive ὅς with the article. πόλεμον δέ is the suffix -δε ‘to’, printed apart: ‘to the war’. ὄπασσε, from ὀπάζω, is ‘gave as companion, sent along’; λαός is ‘people’, the troops.

sentences.t: πᾶν δ’ ἦμαρ μάρναντο περὶ Σκαιῇσι πύλῃσι·
sentences.l: All day long they were fighting around the Scaean Gates;
sentences.i: All day long they fought around the Scaean Gates;
sentences.n: πᾶν ἦμαρ is an accusative of time, ‘all day long’. μάρναντο is the unaugmented imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’; the subject is the two armies. Σκαιῇσι πύλῃσι, with the epic dative plural, is ‘the Scaean Gates’, the gate of Troy toward the plain; the name’s meaning is not certain, ‘left’ or ‘western’ being the usual guesses.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν αὐτῆμαρ πόλιν ἔπραθον, εἰ μὴ Ἀπόλλων
πολλὰ κακὰ ῥέξαντα Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμον υἱὸν
ἔκταν’ ἐνὶ προμάχοισι καὶ Ἕκτορι κῦδος ἔδωκε.
sentences.l:
and now they would have sacked the city on that very day, if Apollo
had not, when he had done many evils, Menoetius’ sturdy son
killed among the front-fighters, and given glory to Hector.
sentences.i: and they would have sacked the city that very day, had not Apollo killed Menoetius’ sturdy son among the foremost fighters, after he had done the Trojans much harm, and given glory to Hector.
sentences.n: καί νύ κεν … ἔπραθον, εἰ μή … ἔκταν’ is a past unreal condition: ‘and they would have sacked…, if … had not killed’. ἔπραθον is an aorist of πέρθω ‘sack’, with ρα for ερ by metathesis, and αὐτῆμαρ is ‘on that very day’. ῥέξαντα, aorist participle of ῥέζω ‘do’, belongs to Patroclus: ‘having done many evils’, to the Trojans. ἔκταν’ is ἔκτανε, aorist of κτείνω. Thetis gives the death to Apollo, who struck Patroclus first; Euphorbus and Hector struck after him.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκα νῦν τὰ σὰ γούναθ’ ἱκάνομαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα
υἱεῖ ἐμῷ ὠκυμόρῳ δόμεν ἀσπίδα καὶ τρυφάλειαν
καὶ καλὰς κνημῖδας ἐπισφυρίοις ἀραρυίας
καὶ θώρηχ’·
sentences.l:
Therefore now to your knees I come, in case you may be willing
to my son, swift-doomed, to give a shield and a helm
and fine greaves, with ankle-clasps fitted,
and a breastplate;
sentences.i: That is why I have come now to your knees, in the hope that you may be willing to give my son, swift to his doom, a shield and a helmet and fine greaves fitted with ankle-clasps, and a breastplate;
sentences.n: The first line is a suppliant’s formula that stands also in the Odyssey, and it keeps the English it has there. To come to someone’s knees is to supplicate him. αἴ κ’ is εἰ with κε, ‘in case, in the hope that’, with ἐθέλῃσθα, a subjunctive with the old second-person ending -σθα. δόμεν is an epic infinitive (= δοῦναι). ὠκυμόρῳ is ‘swift-doomed’, the house rendering. Then four pieces of armour: ἀσπίς ‘shield’, τρυφάλεια ‘helm’, κνημῖδες ‘greaves’, and θώρηξ ‘breastplate’, elided to θώρηχ’ before the rough breathing of ὅ. ἐπισφυρίοις ἀραρυίας is ‘fitted with ankle-clasps’, ἀραρυίας being the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’.

sentences.t:
ὃ γὰρ ἦν οἱ ἀπώλεσε πιστὸς ἑταῖρος
Τρωσὶ δαμείς·
sentences.l:
for what was his, his faithful companion lost,
subdued by the Trojans;
sentences.i: for what he had, his faithful companion lost when he was overcome by the Trojans;
sentences.n: ὃ γὰρ ἦν οἱ is ‘for what was his’, literally ‘what was to him’, with ὅ as the relative and οἱ a dative of possession. ἀπώλεσε is the aorist of ἀπόλλυμι ‘lose’. πιστὸς ἑταῖρος ‘faithful companion’ is Patroclus. δαμείς is the aorist passive participle of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, with the dative Τρωσί ‘by the Trojans’.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ κεῖται ἐπὶ χθονὶ θυμὸν ἀχεύων.
sentences.l: and he lies upon the earth, grieving in heart.”
sentences.i: and my son lies on the earth, grieving at heart.”
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Achilles now, who at 26–27 threw himself on the ground at the news. κεῖται ‘lies’ is the same verb Thetis used of Peleus at 435: father and son both lie helpless. θυμὸν ἀχεύων ‘grieving in heart’ has θυμόν as an accusative of respect; ἀχεύω is a by-form of ἀχέω ‘grieve’. Thetis’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις·
sentences.l: Her then answered the very-famous both-limbed one:
sentences.i: Then the very famous both-limbed god answered her:
sentences.n: The reply formula for Hephaestus, used at 393. τήν is ‘her’, now Thetis. The meaning of ἀμφιγυήεις is unknown; ‘both-limbed’ follows its formation, and the old guesses are ‘lame in both legs’ or ‘skilled with both hands’.

sentences.t: θάρσει· μή τοι ταῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι μελόντων.
sentences.l: “Take courage, let not these things be a care to you in your mind.
sentences.i: “Take courage; do not let these things weigh on your mind.
sentences.n: The line stands also in the Odyssey, with a comma where the edition here prints a raised stop, and it keeps the English it has there. θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω ‘take courage’. μή … μελόντων is a prohibition in the third person: μελόντων is the plural imperative of μέλω ‘be a care to’. τοι is ‘to you’, and φρεσὶ σῇσι ‘your mind’ has the possessive σός in the epic dative plural.

sentences.t:
αἲ γάρ μιν θανάτοιο δυσηχέος ὧδε δυναίμην
νόσφιν ἀποκρύψαι, ὅτε μιν μόρος αἰνὸς ἱκάνοι,
ὥς οἱ τεύχεα καλὰ παρέσσεται, οἷά τις αὖτε
ἀνθρώπων πολέων θαυμάσσεται, ὅς κεν ἴδηται.
sentences.l:
If only I could so surely from ill-sounding death
hide him away, when his fearsome doom should come to him,
as fine armour will be at hand for him, such as anyone in turn
of many men will marvel at, whoever sees it.”
sentences.i: If only I could hide him away from ill-sounding death, when his fearsome doom comes to him, as surely as he will have fine armour, such that any one of many men will marvel at it, whoever sees it.”
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ with the optative δυναίμην is a wish, ‘if only I could’. ὧδε ‘so’ is answered by ὥς ‘as’ in 466: ‘as surely as’. θανάτοιο δυσηχέος is ‘from ill-sounding death’, the genitive of separation with νόσφιν ἀποκρύψαι ‘hide away’. ὅτε … ἱκάνοι, an optative after a wish, is ‘when … should come’. μόρος is ‘doom’ and αἰνός ‘fearsome’. παρέσσεται is the future of πάρειμι ‘be at hand’. θαυμάσσεται is a future of θαυμάζω ‘marvel at’, and ὅς κεν ἴδηται ‘whoever sees it’ is a general relative with the subjunctive. Hephaestus knows he cannot save Achilles, and says so in the form of a wish.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν τὴν μὲν λίπεν αὐτοῦ, βῆ δ’ ἐπὶ φύσας·
sentences.l: So having spoken, her he left on the spot, and went to the bellows;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and left her there, and went to the bellows;
sentences.n: The line is the one at 4.292, with τήν ‘her’ for τούς ‘them’ and ἐπὶ φύσας ‘to the bellows’ for μετ’ ἄλλους, and keeps that English. λίπεν is the unaugmented aorist of λείπω, and αὐτοῦ is an adverb, ‘right there’. βῆ is ‘went’.

sentences.t: τὰς δ’ ἐς πῦρ ἔτρεψε κέλευσέ τε ἐργάζεσθαι.
sentences.l: and these toward the fire he turned and bade them work.
sentences.i: and he turned them toward the fire and told them to work.
sentences.n: τάς ‘these’ is the bellows (φῦσαι, feminine). ἔτρεψε is the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’. κέλευσε, unaugmented, is ‘bade’, and ἐργάζεσθαι ‘to work’ is said of the bellows as if they could hear: like the tripods of 376 and the golden handmaids, Hephaestus’ tools move at his bidding.

sentences.t:
φῦσαι δ’ ἐν χοάνοισιν ἐείκοσι πᾶσαι ἐφύσων
παντοίην εὔπρηστον ἀϋτμὴν ἐξανιεῖσαι,
ἄλλοτε μὲν σπεύδοντι παρέμμεναι, ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε,
ὅππως Ἥφαιστός τ’ ἐθέλοι καὶ ἔργον ἄνοιτο.
sentences.l:
And the bellows, twenty, in the crucibles all were blowing,
sending forth every kind of well-kindling blast,
at one time to be at hand for him as he hurried, at another again otherwise,
however Hephaestus wished and the work went forward.
sentences.i: And the bellows, twenty in all, were blowing into the crucibles, sending out every kind of blast to kindle the fire, now to be at hand for him as he hurried, now again otherwise, however Hephaestus wished and the work went forward.
sentences.n: ἐφύσων is the imperfect of φυσάω ‘blow’, with φῦσαι ‘bellows’ as subject, ἐείκοσι (= εἴκοσι) ‘twenty’. χόανοι are ‘crucibles’, the pots in which metal is melted (from χέω ‘pour’). ἀϋτμή is ‘breath, blast’, and εὔπρηστος ‘well-kindling’ is from πρήθω ‘blow up (a fire)’. Line 472 is short in expression: παρέμμεναι (= παρεῖναι) ‘to be at hand’ says what the bellows were for, and ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε leaves the other case to be understood, ‘at other times (blowing) otherwise’. ἄνοιτο is the optative of ἄνω ‘accomplish’, passive in sense, ‘the work was being done’.

sentences.t:
χαλκὸν δ’ ἐν πυρὶ βάλλεν ἀτειρέα κασσίτερόν τε
καὶ χρυσὸν τιμῆντα καὶ ἄργυρον·
sentences.l:
And bronze into the fire he threw, unwearied, and tin
and precious gold and silver;
sentences.i: He threw unwearied bronze into the fire, and tin, and precious gold and silver;
sentences.n: βάλλεν is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘threw’. ἀτειρέα ‘unwearied’ is the house rendering of the bronze’s epithet, though it stands apart from χαλκόν here. κασσίτερος is ‘tin’. τιμῆντα is contracted from τιμήεντα ‘valued, precious’. These are the four metals of the shield.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
θῆκεν ἐν ἀκμοθέτῳ μέγαν ἄκμονα, γέντο δὲ χειρὶ
ῥαιστῆρα κρατερήν, ἑτέρηφι δὲ γέντο πυράγρην.
sentences.l:
and then
he set on the anvil-block a great anvil, and took in his hand
a strong hammer, and in the other he took the fire-tongs.
sentences.i: and then he set a great anvil on the anvil-block, and took a strong hammer in one hand and the fire-tongs in the other.
sentences.n: θῆκεν is the aorist of τίθημι ‘set’. ἀκμοθέτῳ is the block of 410, and ἄκμονα ‘anvil’. γέντο is an old aorist meaning ‘took, grasped’, found only in this form. ῥαιστήρ, from ῥαίω ‘shatter’, is the ‘hammer’, here feminine, as κρατερήν ‘strong’ shows. ἑτέρηφι is ‘with the other (hand)’, with the old suffix -φι used for a dative. πυράγρη is ‘fire-tongs’, for holding the hot metal.

sentences.t:
ποίει δὲ πρώτιστα σάκος μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε
πάντοσε δαιδάλλων, περὶ δ’ ἄντυγα βάλλε φαεινὴν
τρίπλακα μαρμαρέην, ἐκ δ’ ἀργύρεον τελαμῶνα.
sentences.l:
And he made first of all a shield, great and stout,
working it intricately on every side, and around it he threw a rim, shining,
threefold, gleaming, and from it a silver strap.
sentences.i: First of all he made a shield, great and stout, working it intricately on every side, and he set a shining rim round it, threefold and gleaming, and from it hung a silver shield-strap.
sentences.n: ποίει is the unaugmented imperfect of ποιέω ‘make’, and πρώτιστα ‘first of all’ leads the making of the armour. σάκος μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε ‘a shield, great and stout’ is the house phrase. δαιδάλλων is ‘working intricately’, from the same root as δαίδαλα ‘intricate works’ (482). περὶ … βάλλε is ‘threw around’; ἄντυξ is the ‘rim’. τρίπλαξ is ‘threefold’, perhaps three bands of metal. ἐκ δ’ … τελαμῶνα has the verb understood: ‘and from it (he fixed) a silver strap’, the strap on which the shield is carried.

sentences.t: πέντε δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτοῦ ἔσαν σάκεος πτύχες·
sentences.l: And five were the folds of the shield itself;
sentences.i: The shield itself had five layers;
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ … σάκεος ‘of the shield itself’ sets the body of the shield against its rim and strap. πτύχες ‘folds’ are its layers, laid one over another; what they were made of is not said here.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐν αὐτῷ
ποίει δαίδαλα πολλὰ ἰδυίῃσι πραπίδεσσιν.
sentences.l:
and on it
he made many intricate works with knowing wits.
sentences.i: and on it he made many intricate works with his skilled wits.
sentences.n: ἐν αὐτῷ is ‘on it’, the face of the shield. δαίδαλα πολλά ‘many intricate works’ is the house phrase. ἰδυίῃσι πραπίδεσσιν is the formula used of Hephaestus at 1.608 and 380: ἰδυίῃσι is the perfect participle of οἶδα, ‘knowing’, in the epic dative plural, and πραπίδες are ‘wits’.

sentences.t:
ἐν μὲν γαῖαν ἔτευξ’, ἐν δ’ οὐρανόν, ἐν δὲ θάλασσαν,
ἠέλιόν τ’ ἀκάμαντα σελήνην τε πλήθουσαν,
ἐν δὲ τὰ τείρεα πάντα, τά τ’ οὐρανὸς ἐστεφάνωται,
sentences.l:
On it he made the earth, on it the heaven, on it the sea,
and the sun, untiring, and the moon, full,
and on it all the constellations with which the heaven is wreathed,
sentences.i: On it he made the earth, the heaven and the sea, the untiring sun and the full moon, and all the constellations with which the heaven is wreathed,
sentences.n: Each ἐν is an adverb, ‘on it’, the word with which every scene on the shield begins. ἔτευξ’ is ἔτευξε, aorist of τεύχω ‘make’. ἀκάμαντα ‘untiring’ is the sun’s epithet, and σελήνη πλήθουσα is the ‘full’ moon, the participle of πλήθω ‘be full’. τείρεα are ‘constellations’, a word found only in the plural, and ἐστεφάνωται is a perfect passive of στεφανόω ‘crown, wreathe’, so the stars ring the sky like a wreath; the same form is ‘is wreathed’ of Terror round the aegis at 5.739. The sentence goes on through 489.

sentences.t:
Πληϊάδας θ’ Ὑάδας τε τό τε σθένος Ὠρίωνος
Ἄρκτόν θ’, ἣν καὶ Ἄμαξαν ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσιν,
sentences.l:
the Pleiades and the Hyades and the strength of Orion,
and the Bear, which they also call by name the Wagon,
sentences.i: the Pleiades, the Hyades and the strength of Orion, and the Bear, which men also call by name the Wagon,
sentences.n: The constellations are named. τὸ σθένος Ὠρίωνος ‘the strength of Orion’ is a way of naming Orion himself, the hunter, by his strength. Line 487 stands, with one small difference of printing, in the Odyssey (5.273), and the English follows it there. ἐπίκλησιν is an adverbial accusative, ‘by name, as a name’. Ἄμαξα is the ‘Wagon’, the same stars seen as a cart.

sentences.t:
ἥ τ’ αὐτοῦ στρέφεται καί τ’ Ὠρίωνα δοκεύει,
οἴη δ’ ἄμμορός ἐστι λοετρῶν Ὠκεανοῖο.
sentences.l:
which turns in its own place and watches Orion,
and alone has no share in the baths of Ocean.
sentences.i: which wheels round in the same place and keeps watch on Orion, and alone has no share in the baths of Ocean.
sentences.n: The two lines stand also in the Odyssey (5.274–275), and keep the English they have there. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there, in the same place’: the Bear circles the pole. δοκεύει ‘watches’, as it faces Orion across the sky. ἄμμορος is ἄμορος ‘without a share’, with the genitive λοετρῶν (= λουτρῶν) ‘baths’. Ὠκεανός is the river round the earth, into which the setting stars sink; the Bear never sets.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ δύω ποίησε πόλεις μερόπων ἀνθρώπων
καλάς.
sentences.l:
And on it he made two cities of speech-dividing men,
fine ones.
sentences.i: And on it he made two fine cities of men of articulate speech.
sentences.n: ποίησε is the aorist of ποιέω ‘make’. δύω (= δύο) ‘two’. μερόπων ἀνθρώπων is a formula whose meaning is not known; the house rendering ‘speech-dividing’ follows the ancient explanation, ‘with articulate speech’. καλάς ‘fine’ is held over to the next line. What follows describes the first city, at peace; the second comes in the next part.

sentences.t:
ἐν τῇ μέν ῥα γάμοι τ’ ἔσαν εἰλαπίναι τε,
νύμφας δ’ ἐκ θαλάμων δαΐδων ὕπο λαμπομενάων
ἠγίνεον ἀνὰ ἄστυ, πολὺς δ’ ὑμέναιος ὀρώρει·
sentences.i: In the one there were weddings and banquets: they were leading the brides from their chambers through the town under blazing torches, and the wedding-song rose loud;
sentences.n: ἐν τῇ μέν is ‘in the one’, the first city. γάμοι are ‘weddings’ and εἰλαπίναι ‘banquets’. νύμφη is ‘bride’, and the brides are taken to their husbands’ houses. δαΐδων ὕπο λαμπομενάων is ‘under blazing torches’, with the preposition after its noun; the procession is at night. ἠγίνεον is the imperfect of ἀγινέω, an epic form of ἄγω ‘lead’, with no subject expressed. ὑμέναιος is the ‘wedding-song’, and ὀρώρει the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘had risen’. In 493 ἠγίνεον is sounded as three syllables, its εο run together (synizesis), and ὑμέναιος has its first syllable short; read so, the line scans regularly.

sentences.t:
κοῦροι δ’ ὀρχηστῆρες ἐδίνεον, ἐν δ’ ἄρα τοῖσιν
αὐλοὶ φόρμιγγές τε βοὴν ἔχον·
sentences.l:
and young men, dancers, were whirling, and among them
pipes and lyres kept up their sound;
sentences.i: young men were whirling in the dance, and among them pipes and lyres kept up their sound;
sentences.n: κοῦροι is ‘young men’, and ὀρχηστῆρες ‘dancers’ is in apposition. ἐδίνεον is the imperfect of δινέω ‘whirl, spin’. ἐν δ’ ἄρα τοῖσιν is ‘and among them’. αὐλοί are ‘pipes’, reed instruments, and φόρμιγγες ‘lyres’. βοὴν ἔχον is literally ‘held a cry’, ‘kept up their sound’: βοή is any loud sound.

sentences.t:
αἳ δὲ γυναῖκες
ἱστάμεναι θαύμαζον ἐπὶ προθύροισιν ἑκάστη.
sentences.l:
and the women,
standing, were marvelling, at their forecourts, each one.
sentences.i: and the women stood, each at her own forecourt, and marvelled.
sentences.n: αἳ δὲ γυναῖκες is ‘and the women’, the article still pointing like a pronoun. ἱστάμεναι is the present participle of ἵσταμαι ‘stand’. θαύμαζον is the unaugmented imperfect, ‘were marvelling’. ἐπὶ προθύροισιν is ‘at the forecourts’, the space before each house door, and ἑκάστη ‘each one’ is singular beside the plural verb.

sentences.t: λαοὶ δ’ εἰν ἀγορῇ ἔσαν ἀθρόοι·
sentences.l: And the people were in the assembly-place, all together;
sentences.i: And the people were gathered all together in the place of assembly;
sentences.n: λαοί is ‘people’. εἰν is an epic form of ἐν, and ἀγορή is here the place where the assembly meets. ἀθρόοι is ‘all together, in a crowd’. A new scene begins, still in the first city.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ νεῖκος
ὠρώρει, δύο δ’ ἄνδρες ἐνείκεον εἵνεκα ποινῆς
ἀνδρὸς ἀποφθιμένου·
sentences.i: and there a quarrel had arisen: two men were quarrelling over the requital for a man who had perished;
sentences.n: νεῖκος is ‘quarrel’, and ὠρώρει, the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι, is ‘had arisen’ as in 493. ἐνείκεον, imperfect of νεικέω, is ‘were quarrelling’, the verb of the same root. εἵνεκα ποινῆς is ‘for the sake of the requital’: ποινή is the payment owed for a man’s death, made by the killer to his kin. ἀνδρὸς ἀποφθιμένου is ‘for a man who had perished’, from ἀποφθίνω.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν εὔχετο πάντ’ ἀποδοῦναι
δήμῳ πιφαύσκων, ὃ δ’ ἀναίνετο μηδὲν ἑλέσθαι·
sentences.l:
the one was vowing to pay back everything,
making it known to the people, and the other was rejecting taking anything;
sentences.i: the one man vowed to pay back everything, declaring it to the people, and the other rejected the offer and would take nothing;
sentences.n: ὃ μέν … ὃ δέ is ‘the one … the other’. The two lines can be read two ways, and both go back to antiquity. The English takes εὔχετο as ‘vowed’ with ἀποδοῦναι ‘to pay back’, and ἀναίνετο as ‘rejected’ with μηδὲν ἑλέσθαι ‘taking anything’: the killer offers the full price and the dead man’s kinsman will not accept it. The other reading takes εὔχετο as ‘claimed’ and ἀναίνετο as ‘denied’: the one claimed he had paid everything, the other denied he had received anything. πιφαύσκων is ‘making it known’, and δήμῳ ‘to the people’. ἑλέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of αἱρέω ‘take’.

sentences.t: ἄμφω δ’ ἱέσθην ἐπὶ ἴστορι πεῖραρ ἑλέσθαι.
sentences.l: and both were eager before an arbiter to take an end.
sentences.i: and both were eager to have the matter settled before an arbiter.
sentences.n: ἄμφω ‘both’ and ἱέσθην are duals: ἱέσθην is the imperfect of ἵεμαι ‘be eager’. ἴστωρ, from the root of οἶδα ‘know’, is ‘one who knows’, someone who can settle the case; whether he is one of the elders in 503 or another man is not said. πεῖραρ is ‘end, limit’, and πεῖραρ ἑλέσθαι is ‘to get an end’ to the quarrel, a decision.

sentences.t: λαοὶ δ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἐπήπυον ἀμφὶς ἀρωγοί·
sentences.l: And the people were shouting applause for both, on either side helpers;
sentences.i: The people were cheering both of them, taking sides as supporters of each;
sentences.n: ἐπήπυον is the imperfect of ἐπηπύω ‘shout applause, cheer on’, with the dative ἀμφοτέροισιν ‘for both’. ἀμφὶς ἀρωγοί is ‘helpers on either side’: the crowd is divided, some for one man and some for the other.

sentences.t: κήρυκες δ’ ἄρα λαὸν ἐρήτυον·
sentences.l: and heralds were restraining the people;
sentences.i: and heralds were holding the people back;
sentences.n: κήρυκες are ‘heralds’, who keep order in the assembly and, as the next lines show, hand the speaker his sceptre. ἐρήτυον is the imperfect of ἐρητύω ‘restrain, hold back’: the crowd is pressing in on the two men.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ γέροντες
εἵατ’ ἐπὶ ξεστοῖσι λίθοις ἱερῷ ἐνὶ κύκλῳ,
σκῆπτρα δὲ κηρύκων ἐν χέρσ’ ἔχον ἠεροφώνων·
sentences.i: and the elders sat on polished stones in a sacred circle, holding in their hands sceptres from the loud-voiced heralds;
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ γέροντες is ‘and the elders’. εἵατ’ is εἵατο, an epic third plural of ἧμαι ‘sit’ (Attic ἧντο). ξεστοῖσι λίθοις is ‘on polished stones’, the seats of the court, and ἱερῷ ἐνὶ κύκλῳ ‘in a sacred circle’. The sceptre is held by whoever speaks, and the heralds hand it to them. ἠερόφωνος is of uncertain meaning: it is built from ἀήρ ‘air’ (or ‘mist’) and φωνή ‘voice’, and is usually taken as ‘loud-voiced’, which the reading layer follows; the literal layer keeps the formation, ‘air-voiced’. χέρσ’ is χερσί ‘hands’, elided.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν ἔπειτ’ ἤϊσσον, ἀμοιβηδὶς δὲ δίκαζον.
sentences.l: With these then they sprang up, and in turn they gave judgement.
sentences.i: Holding these they rose one after another, and in turn gave their judgement.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν ‘with these’ is the sceptres. ἤϊσσον is the imperfect of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, spring up’: each elder rises quickly to speak. ἀμοιβηδίς is ‘in turn’, and δίκαζον the imperfect of δικάζω ‘give judgement’.

sentences.t:
κεῖτο δ’ ἄρ’ ἐν μέσσοισι δύω χρυσοῖο τάλαντα,
τῷ δόμεν ὃς μετὰ τοῖσι δίκην ἰθύντατα εἴποι.
sentences.l:
And there lay in their midst two talents of gold,
to give to him who among them should speak justice most straightly.
sentences.i: And two talents of gold lay in the middle, to be given to the one among them who should speak justice most straightly.
sentences.n: κεῖτο is ‘lay’. ἐν μέσσοισι is ‘in the middle’, with the epic double σ. δύω χρυσοῖο τάλαντα is ‘two talents of gold’, a weight of gold, not a coin. τῷ δόμεν ‘to give to him’ is an infinitive of purpose (δόμεν = δοῦναι). μετὰ τοῖσι ‘among them’ is probably the elders, the best judge winning the gold; some take it of the two men. δίκην … εἴποι is ‘should speak justice’, and ἰθύντατα, the superlative adverb of ἰθύς ‘straight’, is ‘most straightly’. The description of the first city goes on in the next part.
